title: Hello, what's your name?
title_target: Dober dan! Kako ti je ime?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day and the right level of politeness, say your name, ask how someone is, and see for the first time that Slovenian verbs have THREE number lanes, not two.
bekal: greet people with *dober dan*, *dobro jutro*, *živjo*, and *pozdravljeni*, each in its proper place
say your name with *ime mi je…* or *jaz sem…*, and ask other people theirs
use the verb *biti* for one person — and recognize the two other lanes waiting for you in unit 3

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Prvi dan v jezikovni šoli
dialogs.intro: The first day of a language course at a jezikovna šola in Ljubljana. Two new students sit next to each other.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Dober dan! Kako ti je ime?

lines.text: Dober dan! Ime mi je Budi. Pa ti?
lines.id: Hello! My name is Budi. And you?
lines.literal: good day! name to-me is Budi. and you?

lines.speaker: Budi:

notes: **Kako ti je ime? is not "what is your name".** Literally it is "how to-you is name?" — your name is treated as something that *is with you*, not something *you have*. The answer follows the same shape: *Ime mi je Budi* ("name to-me is Budi"). Shorter and just as correct: *Jaz sem Budi*. The polite form swaps *ti* for *vam*: **Kako vam je ime?**

**Me veseli has no subject.** Literally "(it) pleases me" — there is no "I" and no "it" in it. Slovenian is full of sentences like this, and the same pattern comes back in unit 15 for "my head hurts". The long form is *Me veseli, da sva se spoznala* — for now, the two words are enough.

**Ja and da both mean "yes".** *Ja* was borrowed from German and is used all day in casual talk; *da* sounds tidier and shows up more in writing or with people you treat formally. There is only one opposite: *ne*.

**Slovenka and Slovenec are two different words.** Slovenian makes you pick a gender for every nationality: *Slovenec* (man), *Slovenka* (woman), *Indonezijec* and *Indonezijka*, *Kitajec* and *Kitajka*. English never asks for this, so get used to learning both forms together from now on, not just one.

**Se vidiva — your first peek at dvojina.** Look at the ending: *-va*. That is not a plural, it is the form for **exactly two people**. If three people were saying goodbye, the sentence would become *se vidimo*. This is the antique that made Slovenian famous, and it gets a unit of its own in unit 3 — for now, just use *se vidiva* as one memorized chunk.

grammars.title: Biti — the verb "to be" with three number lanes
body: The first verb you must master, and your first glimpse of what sets Slovenian apart from the rest of Europe. Verb tables in French, German, or Russian have two number columns: singular and plural. Slovenian has **three**.
after: For this unit you only need the first three rows. The other rows are on display now on purpose, so you know they exist — many books hide them until chapter ten, and their readers get a shock.
Paired forms like *midva / midve* sort by gender: *midve* when **both are women**, *midva* for everything else. The same rule applies to *vidva/vidve* and *onadva/onidve*.

grammars.title: Vikanje — two ways to say "you"
body: Slovenian splits the person you're talking to in two, just like French or German. There is only one thing to remember: the polite form uses a **plural verb**, even for one person.

head: Form
Example
Used with
rows: strangers, older people, shop staff, teachers, doctors

after: The practical rule is simple: **start with vi**, and wait for the Slovenian to offer to switch. The offer usually sounds like *Lahko sva na ti?* — "Can we just use *ti*?" Answering *Ja, seveda!* is always right.
Unlike German, Slovenian *vi* does not have to be capitalized. In formal letters people often write *Vi* with a capital as a sign of respect, but that's a choice, not a rule.

blocks.text: These ten phrases are not grammar to memorize — they are emergency tools. Learn the whole forms now, understand how they're built later.

blocks.text: *Prosim* is the most versatile word in Slovenian. It means "please" when asking, "go ahead" when offering, "you're welcome" after someone thanks you, "hello?" when picking up the phone, and "sorry, what was that?" when you didn't catch something. If you could learn only one word on this page, learn this one.
*Oprostite* is for politely getting a stranger's attention; the informal form is *oprosti*. For a real apology people more often say *Se opravičujem* — but *oprostite* is always safe.

sections.title: Greetings by time of day and politeness

blocks.text: Slovenian sorts greetings along two axes at once: what time it is, and how close you are to the other person. This table covers both.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
When to use
rows: Good day / Hello — the safest polite greeting
Good night — only when parting for the night

blocks.text: *Pozdravljeni* is actually a plural form, and that's exactly why it's polite: you greet one person as if they were more than one. To one close male friend the form is *pozdravljen*, to one female friend *pozdravljena* — but as a beginner, *pozdravljeni* is always correct and never rude.

One habit worth copying: in Slovenia, **walking into a small space means saying hello**. An elevator, a doctor's waiting room, a train compartment, a small village shop — people say *dober dan* to strangers, and staying silent is what feels rude.
